trials.notes: Correctly chose WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), walked tokens with next_token(), skipped only SPAN tag tokens, and used serialize_token() for normalized output. All called APIs are present in the rendered docs. Minor deduction: the get_last_error fallback to normalize($html) would discard the rewrite if unsupported markup were encountered.

Correct processor and no undocumented methods: create_fragment(), next_token(), get_tag(), is_tag_closer(), and serialize_token() are documented. The main API-pattern failure is semantic: it used a skip-depth subtree deletion pattern, so it removed SPAN contents instead of only omitting the SPAN opener/closer tokens. That contradicts the documented serialize_token() wrapper-removal example.

Correctly used the HTML Processor for fragment normalization, walked all tokens, skipped SPAN tag tokens, and appended serialize_token(). All methods are documented. Minor deduction only for weak fallback behavior on processor-creation failure / parser error, though it does not affect the tested cases.

failure_analysis: Trial 2 failed simple, nested-spans, attributes-discarded, adjacent-spans, span-with-block-content, and unclosed-span for the same misconception: it treated "remove the SPAN element" as "remove the SPAN subtree." The code increments $skip_depth on a SPAN opener and suppresses every descendant token until the SPAN closer, so text, child elements, adjacent span text, block/void content, and text inside an unclosed SPAN are all dropped. The responsible documentation area is WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token(), especially the rewrite guidance and its example "Remove every SUP element but keep its contents," which shows the correct general pattern: skip matching tag tokens and serialize everything else. The docs were strong enough for trials 1 and 3, but trial 2 shows that the phrase "skip tokens to remove them" can still be overgeneralized into a subtree-skip algorithm. For unclosed-span specifically, next_token() correctly emits a virtual SPAN closer at end of input; the docs describe that closers are visited for unclosed elements, but they do not explicitly warn that a stateful subtree skip will remain active through all trailing content until that virtual closer.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token() docblock and "Recipe: rewrite while serializing tokens"
doc_gaps.problem: The docs show an unwrap-style example, but they do not explicitly contrast wrapper removal with subtree deletion. A reader can infer that tracking depth and skipping while inside the element is the safer way to "remove" an element.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short distinction: to unwrap/remove only an element's own tags, skip matching opener and closer tokens and serialize descendants; to delete an element and all descendants, record depth at the opener and skip until leaving that subtree. Call out that a skip-depth counter deletes contents.

doc_gaps.problem: It is not emphasized that during a token walk, get_tag() matches both opener and closer tag tokens, while text and descendant tokens have no matching tag name.
doc_gaps.suggestion: In token-rewrite examples, state that `if ( 'X' === $processor->get_tag() ) continue;` skips both wrapper tag tokens and preserves all non-X descendant tokens.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs describe virtual closers for unclosed elements, but not their practical effect on rewrite state machines.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a note that subtree-skip state remains active until parser-reported closers, including virtual end-of-input closers; wrapper-unwrapping filters should skip only the element tag tokens when trailing content must remain.

doc_gaps.problem: Near misses used raw input or normalize($html) as fallbacks. Those policies are documented, but it is easy to miss that they discard token-loop rewrites and may violate contracts requiring modified normalized output.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify in fallback guidance that raw input and normalize($html) intentionally discard emitted changes; examples for string-returning rewriters should name which fallback preserves the function's contract and which does not.
